strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: unreliable captions caused by occlusion and restricted viewpoints. Rendering reconstructed objects and using nearby reliable objects as captioning context is a plausible, useful combination.

Table 1 reports consistent node-precision improvements across eight Replica scenes, averaging 0.82 versus 0.68 for ConceptGraphs, alongside fewer duplicate objects. These results provide encouraging evidence of practical value.

Object-adaptive downsampling is simple and potentially useful. The reported Room 0 mapping time decreases from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per iteration while Table 2 shows broadly comparable segmentation accuracy to ConceptGraphs. The paper also provides qualitative renderings, component ablations, and attribution of its main building blocks.
weaknesses: The central ablation evidence is not reconciled across Figures 3 and 5. Averaging the eight per-scene mF1 values in Figure 5 gives approximately 25.16 for the full pipeline and 25.66 without concatenation, whereas Figure 3 reports 30.78 and 28.09, respectively. Removing concatenation also improves mIoU in five of eight scenes. An alternative aggregation could explain some differences, but none is specified. Consequently, the claim that every component consistently improves performance is insufficiently supported.

The mapping equations and stated threshold raise a substantive soundness concern. Equations 2–3 add spatial overlap to a semantic similarity shifted by 0.5, while Section 4.1 sets the matching threshold to 0.45. Thus, even with zero spatial overlap, a pair with embedding dot product greater than -0.1 can qualify for fusion. Without an additional spatial gate, distinct objects can merge solely through semantic similarity. The manuscript and pseudocode do not explain such a gate or reconcile this behavior with the reported mapping quality.

Evaluation fairness and reliability are insufficiently established. Section 4.2 does not specify annotator counts, agreement, adjudication, or uncertainty estimates, and it is unclear whether baseline captioners use the same foundation models and prompts. Edge comparisons additionally change the permitted relationship vocabulary and connectivity construction; introducing a broad 'near' relation can increase valid-edge counts without demonstrating better prediction of the original relationships. Matched-vocabulary and matched-model comparisons are needed.

The automatic evaluation procedure is ambiguous. Sections 4.3–4.4 describe assigning each ground-truth label to its most likely predicted object, rather than assigning a class to every predicted object; handling of unmatched objects, repeated categories, and conflicting assignments is unspecified. The GPT-4o semantic assigner also lacks its exact prompt and validation against human assignments. These omissions materially limit interpretation and reproducibility of the segmentation and ablation scores.

The uncertainty mechanism assumes that the re-shot caption is a reliable reference, but caption agreement does not establish correctness. Reconstructed objects can retain incomplete geometry or segmentation contamination, and correlated caption errors can receive high confidence. There is no direct evaluation of error detection, calibration, or sensitivity to the fixed 50% reliable-object split. Simpler controls, such as re-shot captioning alone or crop-caption consensus, would help establish the contribution of uncertainty-guided retrieval.

Efficiency and generalization claims exceed the available evidence. Timing is reported for mapping on one scene, without hardware details, variability, or total pipeline cost including rendering and additional VLM/LLM calls. Experiments cover only eight Replica scenes, so robustness to real sensor noise and downstream robotics benefits remain untested. The reported mapping acceleration is useful, but does not establish faster overall scene-graph generation.

Important implementation details remain unspecified despite the reproducibility statement: the number of retained crops, candidate-view sampling, clustering algorithm and parameters, and several prompts. Equation 5 also leaves direction normalization unclear and defines the prior direction opposite to the viewing direction for a camera at the average observed position. These details affect the central view-selection mechanism and require clarification.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: occluded or poorly framed object crops can corrupt semantic aggregation in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs. Rendering reconstructed objects from alternative viewpoints and using nearby objects as context is a plausible, useful approach.

Table 1 reports consistent node-precision improvements across all eight Replica scenes, averaging 0.82 versus 0.68 for ConceptGraphs, alongside fewer duplicate objects. These results provide encouraging evidence for the overall pipeline.

Object-scale-dependent downsampling is a practical contribution. The reported mapping time decreases from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per iteration on Room 0, while Table 2 shows approximately preserved segmentation accuracy relative to ConceptGraphs.

The manuscript attributes its foundation models and mapping backbone, provides fusion pseudocode, and includes component ablations and qualitative examples. The large degradation without re-shot processing suggests that rendered object views are worth further investigation.
weaknesses: The main comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. The paper specifies its own language models but does not establish that the Table 1 baselines use matched models, prompts, or inference budgets. Edge generation also changes the relation vocabulary, adding 'near' and part-of relations. Consequently, higher edge precision and more valid edges are not directly comparable without evaluation under a shared relation vocabulary and candidate-edge protocol.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified. Human evaluation omits annotator counts, judgments per example, agreement, and adjudication procedures. Sections 4.3–4.4 describe assigning each ground-truth label to a predicted object, rather than assigning each predicted object a class; handling repeated categories, unmatched objects, and conflicting assignments is unclear. The GPT-4o assignment prompt and validation are also absent. These ambiguities affect the interpretation and reproducibility of the quantitative evidence.

The ablation summary needs reconciliation with the appendix. Figure 3 reports full-pipeline mRecall of 37.37 and mF1 of 30.78, whereas the corresponding scene averages in Figure 5 are approximately 28.61 and 25.16. A different pooling procedure could explain this, but none is stated. Moreover, removing RAG or concatenation improves several scene-level metrics, so claims of consistently complementary benefits need qualification.

The proposed uncertainty score measures agreement with a rendered-view caption, whose correctness is assumed rather than established. Incorrect reconstructions or shared VLM errors can produce confident agreement, and selecting the highest-similarity cluster further favors agreement with that reference. There is no correctness-versus-uncertainty analysis, sensitivity study of the fixed 50% split, or direct comparison against simply captioning the rendered views. Thus, the evidence does not clearly separate uncertainty estimation from the benefit of additional imagery.

The mapping equations raise a concrete soundness concern. With the stated threshold of 0.45, an object pair with zero spatial overlap and zero embedding dot product receives similarity 0.5 and qualifies for fusion. Neither the text nor Algorithm 1 supplies a spatial gate that prevents this. Equation 5 also defines the viewing and prior directions with opposite orientations, so maximizing their dot product appears inconsistent with the claimed prior alignment; vector normalization is unspecified.

Efficiency evidence is limited to mapping time on one scene, without hardware details or total runtime including rendering, captioning, retrieval refinement, and LLM calls. It supports a local mapping speedup, but does not establish an overall pipeline speedup. Evaluation only on Replica also leaves robustness to real RGB-D reconstruction errors untested.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the stated commitment: the crop count k, clustering algorithm and settings, candidate-view sampling and rendering parameters, and several prompts are deferred to a future code release. Overall, assessed as Algorithms/General, the promising integration and reported gains are outweighed by unresolved evaluation and technical concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: unreliable object captions caused by occlusion and restricted viewpoints. Rendering reconstructed objects and using reliable neighboring objects as context is a coherent, practically motivated approach.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements across eight Replica scenes: average node precision increases from 0.68 for ConceptGraphs to 0.82, alongside fewer duplicate objects and generally more valid objects. These results provide promising evidence of practical value.

Dynamic downsampling is simple and potentially useful: the reported mapping time decreases from 6.65 to 2.49 seconds per iteration on Room 0, while Table 2 shows approximately preserved segmentation accuracy. The manuscript also clearly attributes its principal foundation models and mapping baseline.
weaknesses: The ablation evidence is not sufficiently reconciled. Figure 3 reports full-pipeline mF1 of 30.78 versus 28.09 without concatenation, whereas averaging the eight scene results in Figure 5 gives approximately 25.16 versus 25.66, reversing that comparison. A pooled evaluation could differ from scene averaging, but the aggregation procedure is unspecified. Moreover, removing concatenation improves mF1 in five of eight scenes, weakening the claim that every component consistently helps.

The main evaluation leaves important uncertainty about reliability and fairness. Human annotation lacks annotator counts, agreement statistics, and disagreement-resolution details. It is unclear whether ConceptGraphs baselines use the same language models and prompting budget. Edge comparisons additionally change the relation vocabulary and connectivity procedure; adding 'near' can increase valid-edge counts without demonstrating better recovery of the same relationships. Shared-relation evaluation and per-relation results are needed.

The central uncertainty mechanism measures agreement with a rendered-view caption rather than demonstrated correctness. Incorrect reconstruction or correlated captioning errors can therefore create confidently incorrect references. There is no direct validation of uncertainty against caption errors, sensitivity analysis for the fixed 50% split, or comparison against simply captioning the rendered/composite image without uncertainty-based retrieval. These controls are important for establishing the contribution beyond additional VLM inputs and calls.

Several technical details obstruct reproducibility. Equation 5 defines opposing view and prior directions, so its positive dot-product term appears to favor viewing from the opposite side of the average observed camera position; normalization is also unspecified. Equations 2–3 with a 0.45 matching threshold can accept spatially disjoint objects based on semantic similarity alone unless an additional spatial gate exists. The clustering procedure, number of retained crops, rendering configuration, and full evaluation prompts are not provided.

The automatic evaluation protocol is ambiguous: Sections 4.3–4.4 describe assigning each ground-truth label to a predicted object, without explaining how every predicted object receives a class or how assignment conflicts and unmatched objects are handled. The ablations additionally use GPT-4o as a semantic assigner without validating its assignments. Consequently, their numerical results are difficult to independently interpret or reproduce.

The empirical scope is limited to eight Replica scenes, and the runtime claim is supported by one mapping-stage example without hardware details or end-to-end costs for rendering and language-model inference. This supports a promising mapping optimization, but not yet broad robustness or overall efficiency. Taken together with the evaluation and implementation uncertainties, the evidence does not establish a sufficiently convincing Algorithms/General contribution for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent object descriptions across occluded or constrained views. Combining object-centric re-rendering, caption consistency, and spatially retrieved context is a coherent and potentially useful contribution.

Table 1 demonstrates promising object-recognition improvements across two real-world datasets. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT improves object R@3 from 70.7 to 75.0 and R@10 from 79.1 to 83.0 over OpenFunGraph; the LLaVA variant also improves both metrics, supporting applicability beyond a proprietary model.

The human evaluation provides complementary evidence of semantic quality. Across eight Replica scenes, reported node precision improves from 0.68 to 0.82 and edge precision from 0.82 to 0.91 relative to ConceptGraphs. Three annotators, randomized evaluation units, and reported agreement of κ=0.76 strengthen this evidence.
The manuscript acknowledges offline operation and provides useful initial evidence about practical feasibility through pose perturbations, robot-collected observations, mapping runtime, and API cost.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty interpretation is insufficiently validated. Caption agreement with a re-rendered view measures consistency, but both descriptions can share the same error. Section 3.2 nevertheless treats the lowest-uncertainty half of objects as reliable anchors without measuring error-detection performance, anchor accuracy, or sensitivity to this cutoff. Re-rendering can expose previously observed geometry more clearly, but cannot recover surfaces absent from the reconstruction; the claims of breaking dependence on captured viewpoints and obtaining true semantics are therefore overstated.

The ablations do not isolate the principal algorithmic claims. Removing Reshot changes verification and caption filtering together, without comparing against re-shot captioning alone, ordinary multi-view caption agreement, or best-original-view selection under matched VLM budgets. Dynamic mapping and the modified edge-generation rules are also not separately ablated. Consequently, improvements cannot confidently be attributed to uncertainty-guided retrieval rather than better visual inputs, filtering, or other pipeline changes.

Figure 3 requires reconciliation before its conclusions are convincing. The full pipeline has lower mIoU than w/o Concat in five of eight scenes and lower frequency-weighted mIoU in seven of eight. The displayed scene-average mIoU is approximately 20.63 for the full pipeline versus 21.51 without concatenation, whereas panel (a) reports 23.60 versus 21.41. Pooled metrics could differ from scene averages, but the aggregation procedure is unspecified and the broad claim that every component consistently helps is unsupported by the scene-level results.

Important methodological and evaluation details are missing from the supplied manuscript: the caption clustering algorithm, consensus construction and reliability-score formula, top-k value, precise dynamic overlap rule, rendering configuration, and complete relationship prompts. Main-benchmark node matching and ranking procedures are largely delegated to a cited protocol despite modified ground truths and relation categories. The Replica ablation additionally relies on GPT-4o for semantic assignment without reporting assignment validation. Supplementary material is referenced but is not included in the supplied PDF.

Relationship improvements are mixed and their attribution is unclear. Ours-GPT reduces SceneFun3D edge R@5 from 88.1 to 86.2, ties FunGraph3D edge R@10 at 91.4, and improves its R@5 by only 0.6 points. Since relation categories, connectivity, and prompting also change, these results do not establish the claimed causal benefit from improved nodes. No uncertainty intervals or repeated runs are reported for the smaller gains, and the human comparison omits the stronger OpenFunGraph baseline.

Reliability and deployment claims substantially exceed the evidence. A single pose-noise setting, without equivalent baseline perturbations or component ablations, does not establish exceptional robustness under extreme degradation. Robot deployment is an offline qualitative demonstration without task-success or quantitative degradation measurements. Finally, the repeated claim of hallucination-free graphs conflicts with the reported human precisions of 0.82 for nodes and 0.91 for edges. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, these validation gaps outweigh the promising empirical gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent object descriptions caused by occlusion and restricted viewpoints. Combining object-centric rendering, caption consistency, and spatially retrieved context is a coherent approach with potential value for embodied perception.

Table 1 shows promising object-recognition improvements. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT improves R@3/R@10 from OpenFunGraph’s 70.7/79.1 to 75.0/83.0; the LLaVA variant also improves these metrics to 73.6/81.1, demonstrating that gains are not confined to the GPT-4o configuration.

The human evaluation provides complementary evidence beyond vocabulary-based recall. Across eight Replica scenes, reported node/edge precision improves from ConceptGraphs’ 0.68/0.82 to 0.82/0.91, with fewer duplicate nodes. The stated annotation criteria, three annotators, and agreement measurement on 100 units strengthen this evaluation.

The manuscript attributes its major foundation models and predecessor methods, illustrates the pipeline clearly, and includes component ablations, a pose-noise experiment, and physical data collection. Its explicit acknowledgement that processing is offline is useful.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty mechanism is insufficiently validated. Section 3.2 treats agreement with one rendered-view caption as reliability, but mutually consistent captions can be wrong, and rendering the same reconstructed observations does not provide independent verification. There is no direct analysis of error-detection performance, reliability versus actual correctness, or the accuracy of the selected anchors. Selecting the lowest-uncertainty 50% also guarantees an anchor set regardless of absolute reliability. These gaps matter because reliable anchors are the premise of the refinement stage.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed algorithmic contribution. Removing Reshot simultaneously changes visual evidence and caption filtering; it does not distinguish the benefit of rendering from uncertainty-guided selection. Missing controls include rendered-view captioning without uncertainty filtering, ordinary multi-view consensus, and nearest-neighbor context without uncertainty-based anchor selection. Dynamic mapping, connectivity thresholds, relation vocabulary, and prompting also change, making the claimed attribution of edge improvements to better nodes uncertain. Ablations are confined to Replica rather than the two principal benchmarks.

The ablation evidence is less consistent than the discussion suggests. Although Figure 3(a) reports aggregate gains, removing RAG improves mIoU in five of eight individual scenes, and removing concatenation improves it in six. The aggregation underlying the overall panel is not explained sufficiently to reconcile it with the scene-level pattern. These results warrant a qualified account of when contextual refinement helps, supported by variability estimates, rather than claims that every component contributes consistently.

The breadth of the performance claims exceeds Table 1. Ours-GPT has lower SceneFun3D edge R@5 than OpenFunGraph (86.2 versus 88.1), ties its FunGraph3D edge R@10, and improves FunGraph3D edge R@5 by only 0.6 points. Ours-LLaVA trails OpenFunGraph on all four edge metrics. These are still useful results, but do not establish general relationship-prediction superiority. No uncertainty intervals are supplied for the smaller gains, and the human precision comparison omits the strongest benchmark competitor, OpenFunGraph.

Important implementation and evaluation details are missing from the supplied manuscript. The caption-clustering algorithm, consensus construction, final reliability-score formula, number of retained crops, and exact dynamic overlap/connectivity rules are unspecified. The construction of ranked object predictions from free-form captions also needs clarification. Supplementary parameter analyses, prompts, and runtime profiling are referenced but were not supplied. Consequently, reproducing both the core method and its evaluation would require substantial interpretation.

The stronger reliability and deployment claims are unsupported. Virtual re-shooting can reorganize observed geometry but cannot recover surfaces never captured, so describing it as breaking dependence on the input trajectory is overstated. A single Gaussian perturbation setting of 2 cm/1 degree, without baseline noise comparisons or a severity sweep, does not establish resilience to extreme degradation or accumulated drift. The robot experiment is qualitative and offline, with no task-success measurements or quantified localization comparison. Finally, the repeated 'hallucination-free' characterization is not demonstrated by an evaluation that reports 0.82 node precision and 0.91 edge precision. Assessed as Algorithms/General, the promising empirical gains do not yet outweigh these gaps in mechanism validation and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent object descriptions caused by occlusion and constrained viewpoints. Combining rendered object views with reliability-guided contextual refinement is a coherent and practically motivated contribution.

Object-classification results are promising across two real-world benchmarks. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT improves R@3 from 70.7 to 75.0 and R@10 from 79.1 to 83.0 over OpenFunGraph. The LLaVA variant also improves these metrics, suggesting benefits beyond using a stronger proprietary model.

The human evaluation provides complementary evidence about graph quality. Across eight Replica scenes, reported node precision improves from 0.68 to 0.82 and edge precision from 0.82 to 0.91 over ConceptGraphs, with fewer duplicate nodes. Three annotators, randomized evaluation units, and reported agreement of κ = 0.76 strengthen this evidence.

The manuscript evaluates component removal, pose perturbations, and physical data collection, and explicitly acknowledges offline operation. These experiments provide useful initial evidence of practical feasibility.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty claim is insufficiently validated. Caption agreement with a rendering derived from the same observations measures consistency, which need not imply correctness: both captions can share an error. There is no direct evaluation of error detection, reliability ranking, or the correctness of the selected semantic anchors. Selecting the lowest-uncertainty 50% also guarantees anchors even when an entire scene is unreliable.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate uncertainty-guided refinement from additional visual evidence and caption filtering. Comparisons with rendered-view captioning alone, crop-consistency filtering, and nearest-neighbor context without uncertainty selection would clarify the contribution. Moreover, Fig. 3 shows that removing concatenation improves mIoU in five of eight scenes and f-mIoU in all eight, despite the opposite aggregate result. The aggregation procedure needs explanation, and the claim of consistently complementary components is too strong.

Relationship improvements are mixed and their cause is confounded. Ours-GPT falls below OpenFunGraph on SceneFun3D edge R@5 (86.2 versus 88.1), ties FunGraph3D R@10, and improves FunGraph3D R@5 by only 0.6 points. Meanwhile, edge connectivity, relation categories, and few-shot prompting also change. Without controlled experiments or variability estimates, these results do not establish that improved node captions drive the reported edge gains.

Important methodological details remain unspecified in the supplied manuscript: caption clustering, consensus construction, the final reliability score, top-k selection, and exact dynamic spatial thresholds. Additional details are deferred to supplementary material that was not supplied. These omissions affect reproduction of the central mechanism, rather than merely implementation convenience.

Claims of 'hallucination-free' graphs, extreme-noise resilience, and deployment readiness exceed the evidence. Human precision remains below 1.0; robustness uses a single 2 cm/1° perturbation setting without a baseline comparison under matched noise; and the robot demonstration is offline graph construction without downstream task measurements. Virtual re-rendering can expose accumulated observations but cannot recover surfaces never captured. End-to-end latency and quantitative deployment results are also absent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent object semantics caused by occlusion and cross-view aggregation. Combining object-centric rendering, caption agreement, and contextual refinement is a coherent and potentially useful contribution under Algorithms/General.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across two real-world datasets and two VLM backbones. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT improves object R@3/R@10 from OpenFunGraph’s 70.7/79.1 to 75.0/83.0; the LLaVA variant also improves both object metrics.

The human evaluation complements benchmark recall with precision and duplicate counts. Across eight Replica scenes, reported node precision improves from 0.68 to 0.82 over ConceptGraphs, while edge precision improves from 0.82 to 0.91. Three annotators, randomized evaluation units, and reported agreement strengthen this evidence.

The supplementary material provides useful retrieval ablations, pose and point-density perturbations, prompt examples, mapping pseudocode, and offline deployment details. The misleading re-shot example also acknowledges that rendered observations can be incorrect.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty interpretation is insufficiently validated. Section 3.2 retains only the highest-similarity cluster relative to the re-shot caption, potentially discarding substantial contradictory evidence. Agreement can also be confidently wrong, particularly because rendered and original observations share the same reconstruction inputs. The paper does not directly measure error-detection quality, anchor correctness, or sensitivity to the fixed 50% reliable-object split. The refinement ablations support the pipeline but do not establish that this score reliably measures semantic uncertainty.

The ablation evidence needs reconciliation. In Fig. 3, removing concatenation improves per-scene mF1 in six of eight scenes, despite the aggregate reporting a decline from 30.78 to 28.09. A pooled confusion matrix could differ from scene averaging, but the aggregation procedure is not explained sufficiently to interpret this reversal. Moreover, the strongest component ablations use GPT-4o-mediated semantic assignment on Replica rather than the main real-world benchmark protocol; these assignment decisions are not independently validated.

The active-verification claims exceed what virtual re-rendering establishes. Re-shots reorganize already observed points and can remove surrounding clutter, but cannot recover surfaces never captured. The isolated re-shot baseline performs substantially worse than passive captioning on SceneFun3D. A controlled comparison against strong passive view selection and multi-view prompting, with matched mapping, refinement, and inference budget, is needed to isolate the advantage over existing viewpoint-aware approaches.

The mapping specification contains a consequential reproducibility ambiguity. Algorithm 1 defines semantic similarity as a rescaled dot product, (f_local^T f_global)/2 + 1/2, and adds nonnegative spatial overlap before applying a threshold of 0.45. With normalized embeddings, even zero semantic similarity and zero overlap would exceed this threshold. This differs from the main text’s cosine-similarity description and appears to permit merging spatially unrelated objects. The actual gating and normalization must be clarified.

Relationship improvements are mixed, and their attribution is overstated. Ours-GPT is below OpenFunGraph on SceneFun3D edge R@5 and ties it on FunGraph3D edge R@10. The Ours Node + CG Edge variant also remains below OpenFunGraph across all four edge metrics. These results support some benefits from improved nodes, but do not clearly establish that node correction principally explains the full system’s relationship gains.

The deployment evidence supports offline scene reconstruction rather than demonstrated downstream robotic reliability. The physical evaluation reports node precision without scene/object sample counts or uncertainty estimates, and the pose stress test examines only one noise setting without comparative baseline degradation. Claims of deployment readiness and exceptional resilience should therefore be narrowed. Missing exact model versions, complete few-shot prompts, and repeated-run variability further limit reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: occlusion and inconsistent multi-view captions can corrupt open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs. Combining object-centric renderings with selectively retrieved spatial context is a plausible and useful approach.

Table 1 reports meaningful object-recognition gains on two real-world datasets. Ours-GPT improves FunGraph3D object R@3 from 70.7 to 75.0 and R@10 from 79.1 to 83.0. The LLaVA variant also improves these metrics, providing evidence that the benefits are not solely attributable to GPT-4o.

The human evaluation provides complementary evidence: Replica node precision improves from 0.68 to 0.82 over ConceptGraphs, with fewer duplicates and generally more valid objects. Three annotators, randomized evaluation units, and reported agreement of κ=0.76 strengthen this assessment.

The supplementary material includes useful implementation details, retrieval ablations, a misleading-rendering example, and physical-data evaluation. The explicit acknowledgment that scene-graph generation runs offline helps establish the system's actual deployment scope.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty interpretation is insufficiently validated. Section 3.2 measures agreement with a potentially incorrect re-shot caption and retains only the highest-similarity cluster, discarding conflicting evidence. Agreement can therefore reflect shared error rather than correctness. The bottom half of objects is always refined, regardless of absolute reliability. Table 3 supports selective refinement over refining everything, but does not establish that this score identifies errors better than crop disagreement, segmentation confidence, or random selection at the same refinement budget. Error-detection curves and anchor accuracy would directly test the central claim.

Figure 3 does not support the uniformly positive component interpretation given in the text. Removing concatenation improves per-scene mF1 in five of eight scenes; removing RAG improves it in four, with another tie. Yet the aggregate panel reports clear gains for the full method. Pooled metrics can differ from scene averages, so this is not necessarily an arithmetic error, but the aggregation must be explained and reconciled with the heterogeneous results. Without uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, the claimed consistent complementarity is not established.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the distinctive algorithmic contribution. The passive baseline uses only the three most confident crops, whereas the complete pipeline adds rendering, caption selection, contextual prompting, and additional inference. A matched-budget baseline using stronger observed-view selection or joint multi-view reasoning is missing, despite discussing such approaches in related work. The isolated re-shot baseline performs substantially worse than passive GPT-4o on SceneFun3D object R@3, making a controlled comparison especially important.

Several central claims exceed the evidence. Rendering the reconstructed points can remove background clutter and combine observed surfaces, but cannot recover surfaces never observed; describing this as breaking dependence on the captured trajectory overstates the information available. Likewise, one Gaussian pose-noise setting without corresponding baseline degradation does not establish exceptional robustness to tracking drift. The robot study evaluates offline perception, with no downstream navigation or manipulation success measurements to substantiate deployment-readiness claims.

Relationship improvements are mixed rather than uniformly state of the art. Ours-GPT falls below OpenFunGraph on SceneFun3D edge R@5 (86.2 versus 88.1), ties FunGraph3D R@10, and improves FunGraph3D R@5 by only 0.6 points. The fixed eight-category output vocabulary and BERT mapping also warrant an explicit mapping description to make the comparison interpretable.

Important reproducibility ambiguities remain. Section 3.1 describes raw cosine similarity, whereas Algorithm 1 shifts it to cosine/2 + 1/2 before adding spatial overlap. With the stated merge threshold of 0.45, the latter can permit merging even with zero overlap, materially changing object association. The manuscript also omits portions of the few-shot prompts and does not sufficiently specify rendering/visibility computation or the exact API model versions. These issues affect reproduction of the scientific results, beyond presentation quality.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs: inconsistent object descriptions caused by occlusion and poor viewpoints. Combining object-centric rendering, caption agreement, and nearby semantic context is a coherent and potentially useful contribution.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across two real-world datasets. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT improves object R@3/R@10 from OpenFunGraph’s 70.7/79.1 to 75.0/83.0; the LLaVA variant also improves these metrics, supporting usefulness beyond a stronger proprietary backbone.

weaknesses: The central uncertainty claim lacks direct validation. Section 3.2 measures agreement with the re-shot caption after retaining only the highest-similarity cluster, which can assign high confidence to mutually consistent but incorrect captions. The paper does not measure error-detection performance or anchor correctness across uncertainty levels, and the fixed 50% split is not justified experimentally. Table 3 supports selective refinement but does not establish that this particular score reliably identifies errors.

The aggregate ablation conclusions need reconciliation with the per-scene results. Figure 3 reports overall mF1 of 30.78 versus 28.09 without concatenation, but averaging its eight scene-level values gives approximately 25.16 versus 25.66, and removing concatenation improves mF1 in five scenes. A matched-budget baseline using stronger original-view selection, alongside simpler caption-agreement filtering, would better establish the algorithmic contribution. These limitations would be acceptable with narrower claims.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful supplement: the main crop count k, handling of fewer than three captions during clustering, rendering and visibility details, exact model snapshots and decoding settings, and complete few-shot prompts are not fully specified. Repeated-run variability is also absent, making the smaller benchmark gains difficult to assess.
